Most people assume that a router is a piece of hardware, but that’s not true. The router is actually software, and the hardware is just what that software runs on. Almost anything can be a router, just like anything can be on a cob in that one episode of Rick and Morty. The laptop in the photo is my router, configured in exactly the way this guide describes.

Have you ever wanted to host a server at home or in your office, but you can’t because the ISP won’t give you static IPs? Are you behind a CGNAT? This guide is for you. It will teach you how to route static IPv4 and (native) IPv6 addresses to your network, with hosts directly pingable on the internet and all ports open. With this guide, you won’t need to host your software project on github anymore, because you can instead install gitea/cgit with a mailing list on your raspberry pi and host it in your basement or living room!

I recently moved libreboot.org hosting to a much faster network than what it had before, but the new ISP doesn’t assign static IPv4 or IPv6 subnets on the line, and it has all kinds of restrictions, though speed, uptime and latency are all excellent. I decided therefore to set up a tunnel connection using Andrews & Arnold Ltd (A&A) L2TP tunnel service. This is basically similar to most VPN services, but you get a lot more freedom and flexibility e.g. IPv4 subnets (for example, you could host your own DNS on this).

It could also just be used for normal day to day internet tasks. A&A provide you with an unfiltered service, unshaped and unthrottled in any way.

Adapt this guide according to your distro. Basically all we want to do is do PPP via L2TP and enable packet forwarding in Linux, so that packets can pass between two interfaces. We then set routes. We will have these interfaces:

  • WAN port (ethernet) - upstream ISP
  • tunnel port (ppp over l2tp) - physically via WAN port
  • LAN port (ethernet) - packets ONLY routed between it and the tunnel, NOT the WAN port directly. Routes set accordingly.

L2TP is a protocol used for to tunnel traffic on the internet. It’s quite commonly used by ISPs to connect customers up to their backend, where they then provide a PPP login.

So long as you have an ethernet port available to use for internet, your tunnel router can work nicely. If you need to, you could set up a WiFi connection or 4G tether on another machine, sharing that over an RJ45 ethernet port for your L2TP router to connect to; for example, raspberry pi USB tethered to 4G LTE service via dongle, assigned IPs presumably on NAT+DHCP, via ethernet.

Traffic will be forced, via static route, to A&A’s L2TP tunnel server. In this way, all traffic will go through L2TP and nothing else. It is completely isolated from your main network. With this setup, you can host your servers anywhere, and move them very easily.

You need a computer with 2 ethernet interfaces on it (RJ45). You then need to run either Linux or BSD on that. For the purpose of this tutorial, I will tell you how to configure Debian Linux, but the information here can be adapted for any other system. I really only recommend hosting this on BSD or Linux.

In my case, I had these physical interfaces:

  • enp14s0 is configured via NAT address to normal ISP router, and static route to A&A’s L2TP server. Client-side L2TP shall connect through this
  • eno0 is for routing IPs from the L2TP, to a switch. this is basically my LAN port

Yours may differ, so adapt accordingly.

When you first install Debian on the router, you might aswell just use the net installer. Install only the base system (Standard system utilities selected in tasksel). You might also enable SSH, if you wish.

Before you actually configure the routing, your Debian machine must have internet so that you can download packages. Alternatively, you might have apt configured to fetch them from installation media. It’s up to you, really.

You must install these packages:

apt-get install ppp pppoe xl2tpd iproute2 tcpdump net-tools resolvconf

You should install these packages BEFORE doing anything else. Just connect via DHCP or something and install these. You could also grab them from Debian installation media.

If you need a decent text editor, might I suggest Vim. As scandalous as it may seem, Debian doesn’t install it by default!

MAKE SURE you have the packages installed, as listed above, before continuing. At this point, we dive straight in and configure everything.

For our purposes, the WAN side on the router will connect to the internet via NAT, through the main ISPs network, but we will not use DHCP. Instead, a static (NAT) IP address will be specified, but with no gateway; in so doing, no default route will be set, but we will set a static route.

The static route will only route traffic to 90.155.53.19 which is A&A’s L2TP server, via what would otherwise be a gateway IP, in my case 10.42.0.1, but in your case that might be 192.168.1.1. You must adapt accordingly.

By setting the static route this way, we can only connect to A&A L2TP when the tunnel connection is down. When it’s up, we still have no default route but then we add a default route, going through the PPP tunnel via L2TP. In this way, all traffic (except traffic to 90.155.53.19 directly) will go through the L2TP tunnel, NOT your main upstream ISP (e.g. Virgin, Sky, TalkTalk). By doing this, we ensure that all traffic correctly goes through A&A only.

The reason we use A&A’s IP address directly, is because we don’t have DNS when the L2TP tunnel is down.

Please read the comments in the example below. They are important. You must adapt the config below for your purposes:

source /etc/network/interfaces.d/*

# The loopback network interface
auto lo
iface lo inet loopback

# NOTE: 10.42.0.116 is the normal gateway router, LAN side,
# not anything l2tp-related.
# the 10 addresses below would likely be `192.168.x.x/24` in your case
# adapt accordingly

# NOTE: the IPs on eno0 are /28 subnet ones, assigned by a&a for my l2tp service
# you must adapt these for your own line. please note also a&a typically
# offers a /29 for l2tp but they gave me a /28; for a /29, you should
# use netmask 255.255.255.248, but in my case i specified 255.255.255.240

auto enp14s0
allow-hotplug enp14s0
iface enp14s0 inet static
       address 10.42.0.116
       netmask 255.255.255.0
       network 10.42.0.0
       # gateway 10.42.0.1 # we will set a custom route instead. see below
       broadcast 10.42.0.255
       up /sbin/ip route add 90.155.53.19/32 via 10.42.0.1 dev enp14s0

# LAN
auto eno0
iface eno0 inet static 
   address 81.187.172.129
   netmask 255.255.255.240 
   dns-nameservers 217.169.20.20 217.169.20.21

iface eno0 inet6 static 
   address  2001:8b0:b95:1bb5::1
   netmask 64 
   dns-nameservers 2001:8b0::2020 2001:8b0::2021

# NOTE: because above, we are forcing everything to go over L2TP, we will
# not have DNS until the L2TP is up. this is why the IP address of A&A's
# L2TP router is used directly!

# NOTE: no hardline so PPP not configured here. This is handled via xl2tpd

NOTE: IP address 90.155.53.19 is what l2tp.aa.net.uk resolves to, and it shall be used directly for our purposes, due to absent name resolution during initialisation of this network, when setting up L2TP. The static route that we set, on enp14s0, ensures that we do have internet on the WAN side (to the main ISP, not A&A), assuming that the (physical) main network itself works.

You must permit packet forwarding, so that traffic can flow between the two network interfaces. Edit this file:

Uncomment this line:

#net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

And this line (NOTE: disables stateless address autoconfiguration)

#net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1

The lines should then look like this:

net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1

Now run:

sysctl -p

The last command simply applies it now, but this would also apply during every booting of your system.

It may seem counter-intuitive, that we’re configuring PPP as though we’re on a hardline, but this is important for the next step. A&A provides L2TP without authentication, but then you authenticate via PPP routed through L2TP. It is through PPP that your (public) IP addresses are assigned, when you use A&A. Such is also true of their hardline servers (e.g. VDSL/FTTP).

Debian kernels should already have the correct modules, but otherwise you must ensure that the CONFIG_PPPOL2TP and CONFIG_L2TP options are enabled in your kernel configuration.

It should be noted that A&A L2TP service is (as of this day) currently without IPSEC or other encryption such as wireguard. This is less than ideal, but you will likely be doing a lot of encrypted things online anyway (lots of websites are https-aware nowadays).

As a result of plain L2TP being used, you can get away with hosting this on very weak hardware, and still get full speed. One day, I might write guides for how to use L2TP with, say, IPSEC enabled (using something other than A&A for the upstream L2TP service).

You will not be able to use DNS until the L2TP is up, so we will use A&A’s IP address for l2tp.aa.net.uk directly, which is 90.155.53.19.

Place the following contents:

[lac aaisp]
lns = 90.155.53.19
require authentication = no
pppoptfile = /etc/ppp/options.aaisp

Create this file, and place the following contents:

NOTE: the name and password entries are your A&A login details for L2TP.

+ipv6
ipv6cp-use-ipaddr
name xyz@a.X
password Your_xyz@A.X_password
noauth
ifname ppp-aaisp-l2tp

PPP and L2TP are managed by pppd, which executes if up/down scripts when interfaces go up or down. We shall manipulate this accordingly:

This file sets a default route on IPv6, but it can be (ab)used in general to handle L2TP/PPP going up/down. This file is for when the link goes up. A default route must be set!

The file should contain this logic:

#!/bin/bash
/bin/logger $1 is up
if [ $1 = "ppp-aaisp-l2tp" ]; then
	/bin/logger "AAISP over L2TP circuit is online; adding routes"
	/sbin/ip route add default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link
	/sbin/ip -6 route add default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link
fi

Don’t forget to make it executable:

chmod 755 /etc/ppp/ipv6-up.d/0000-defaultroute

The routes must be deleted, when the line goes down:

#!/bin/bash
/bin/logger $1 is down
if [ $1 = "ppp-aaisp-l2tp" ]; then
	/bin/logger "AAISP over L2TP circuit is offline; removing routes"
	/sbin/ip route del default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link
	/sbin/ip -6 route del default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link
fi

Don’t forget to make this executable aswell:

chmod 755 /etc/ppp/ipv6-down.d/0000-defaultroute

You may notice that we have, thus far, not specified any way in which the L2TP tunnel connection is actually started. This will now be explained.

Create the xl2tpd control file:

mkdir -p /var/run/xl2tpd touch /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control

Start the xl2tpd service:

systemctl start xl2tpd

Enable it at every boot:

systemctl enable xl2tpd

We now have the L2TP daemon starting automatically at boot time, but it will not automatically bring up your connection. The daemon monitors writes to a control file, which we just created at /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control.

Tell the daemon to connect to aaisp:

echo “c aaisp” > /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control

To stop the L2TP connection, do this:

echo “d aaisp” > /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control

By running ip a, you will see the tunnel connection listed as ppp-aaisp-l2tp, but only when the PPP (over L2TP) connection is active. As you saw earlier, we went through the ifup/down scripts in Debian, that add/remove routes.

You need to decide whether you want L2TP automatically starting in your router. In some situations, it may not actually be desirable for it to autostart, like if you just want to quickly test a new network but aren’t ready for it to go in production yet.

You can find useful logs in /var/log/messages, for xl2tpd.

Due to the way xl2tpd works (control files), I concluded that the best way to handle this is with crontab. As root, do:

crontab -e

In there, insert:

* * * * * echo "c aaisp" > /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control

You might also add something like this, for resolving domain names:

* * * * * echo "nameserver 217.169.20.20" > /etc/resolv.conf

This L2TP routing setup is a bit hacky, and this guide could use some refinement. The rule for resolvconf, as above, simply keeps DNS working. The nameserver IP used, in the above example, is provided by A&A for customers.

Running the command when L2TP is up does nothing, and xl2tpd will simply exit on that run, while the tunnel remains open. When the tunnel is down, running that command will bring it back up.

If your connection frequently has drop-outs of a few seconds, xl2tpd re-running every minute will give you a lot more unnecessary down time.

It may be advisable to run every 5 seconds instead. The crontab file does not provide for this, allowing only per minute instructions in our case.

You might simply run a script at boot time, that does it in a five-second loop. For example:

#!/bin/sh

while true
do
	echo "c aaisp" > /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control
	sleep 5
done

A more intelligent way might be to put, in the ifdown script as above, an instruction to run the above loop, but make the loop exit when the tunnel is up. That same modified script would also run at boot time. In this way, you might save an extra second or two, but I wouldn’t bother.

You can simply hook up an ethernet switch, to the 2nd interface on your router, the one that has allocated IPv4/6 subnet addresses on it as per /etc/network/interfaces. Your host will then connect to that switch.

On that ethernet switch, you will then set your host(s) to use an IP address from the /28 or /29 IPv4 subnet. You may even have a bigger subnet than that, if you asked A&A nicely. You can also use IPv6, but without SLAAC; simply set as many static IPv6 addresses that you want, on the host.

With this routing setup, dual stack IPv4 and IPv6 is possible, for any host connected to it.

The internet should Just Work on the router itself. No DHCP or NAT is running, in this configuration; perhaps a guide could be written for that, but for this exact setup as described on the page, you can simply specify the following as static IP address:

  • IP (host): any unused IP address (v4 or v6) on the subnet A&A gave you. Example (for libreboot.org): 81.187.172.132 and 2001:8b0:b95:1bb5::4
  • gateway: the IP of the L2TP router, on LAN side. In the example above, this would be 81.187.172.129 and 2001:8b0:b95:1bb5::1
  • netmask (IPv4): 255.255.255.240 on my /28 subnet. If you have a /29, it should be 255.255.255.248
  • broadcast (IPv4): in my case, I’m on 81.187.172.128/28, so the broadcast address would be 81.187.191.143; 128 is 10000000 in binary, and 32-28 is 4, so we mask the 4 least significant bits which becomes 10001111, which is 143. You need to do the maths, for your specific IP and subnet size.
  • prefix (IPv6): 64

Again, there is no DHCP on this network; additionally, we are not running a DNS resolver (you could run one, if you wish). You must specify one manually. Many resolvers exist. A&A provide them, for customers:

  • 217.169.20.20
  • 217.269.20.21
  • 2001:8b0::2020
  • 2001:8b0::2021

You should configure SSH to accept keys only and (optional) only listen on a local IP address (e.g. 10 network). This is beyond the scope of the article, but it’s quite trivial to set up.

e.g.

ListenAddress 10.0.0.42

The following commands may be useful later, to debug issues:

ip route
ip -6 route
ping 8.8.8.8
ping6 2001:4860:4860::8888
tcpdump -ni eno0

Your main ISP (that you use to then run L2TP through) most likely doesn’t support higher than 1500 MTU, if that. Your L2TP connection will add bytes in a frame, so the encapsulated PPP connection will have a lower MTU. There is no way to avoid this, unless you have a hypothetical ISP that can give you, say, 1540 MTU or something like that.

Anyway, the result is that your packets will be fragmented. In your A&A control panel login (see: https://control.aa.net.uk/), you can set MTU manually but I just recommend leaving it on auto.

If you see an MTU of, say, 1460, on your PPP connection (when SSH’d into the router and running ip a or something), don’t worry, it’s normal. Just let your router handle it, it’s what Linux was born to do.

Sometimes called reverse DNS.

In an IP address, the PTR record resolves back to an arbitrary domain name which can be set. Typically, your ISP will assign one and that’s all you get, but A&A lets you change it in the control panel: https://control.aa.net.uk/

You must get your domain name added to your login, even if it’s not actually registered with A&A. Simply email their tech team and ask them to do it. You could also just ask them to set the PTR records.

For example, A/AAAA records in your DNS for foo.bar.com might point to one of your IPs, and then you’d make that IP point back to foo.bar.com. You can do this for an IPv4 and an IPv6 address that A&A assigns to you.

This can be very useful when running mail servers, precisely because you can make the same entry for both IPv4 and IPv6. For example, my mail server has the PTR record, on IPv4 and IPv6, of libreland.libreboot.org and I specify this in my mail server plus DNS server configurations; the IP is also set in my SPF record, with A/AAAA records for that IP pointing to libreland.libreboot.org, so that everything matches up. This, plus other things like setting proper DKIM record, is essential when running a mail server, because a lot of services (like GMail) will block you on suspicion of spam if these are misconfigured.

My next guide may in fact be how to set up a mail server! Also DNS and web, etc.

I will not configure a firewall on this network. I always get an IPv4 subnet from a&a either on hardlines or L2TP, and I run an open network. The router is always hardened to only allow local SSH connections, or SSH turned off, for security.

No NAT/DHCP either. If local hosts want to firewall themselves, they can, and they can provide that stuff. I really don’t see the point in using DHCP for public IPv4 subnets.

If I want NAT/DHCP inside such a network, I usually plug in an OpenWRT router and set a static IP on the WAN port for that. I also use OpenWRT routers to in this way, when I want to set up a WiFi connection behind A&A.

Essentially, I like my main network to be “invisible”. Just plug in and set an IP (from the public subnet) and you’re good to go. This assumes you have good physical security and/or you trust the people that have access to it.

In short, this is a real internet connection. Anything you plug into this network will be directly on the internet. You should consider your security model, when doing this. It is especially important to consider physical security; who do you trust, if you’re running this at your company (or even your own home)?

You should not connect anything insecure directly to this main network. For iexample, your playstation or proprietary shitware Windows PC are not to be trusted. A secure linux/BSD machine, assuming you’re competent, is absolutely fine. This setup is intended for sysadmins who really want to host lots of servers on their home network.

You might configure codel which is nice for QoS but that’s beyond the scope of this article.

The /tmp, /var/run and /var/lock directories should also be tmpfs. This isn’t strictly necessary, but for a high-performance machine it might be desirable, especially for something like this.

If you’re running this on really slow hardware, you might consider that, but you must also take memory usage into account when relying on tmpfs.

It should be noted that A&A L2TP service is (as of this day) currently without IPSEC or other encryption such as wireguard. This is less than ideal, but you will likely be doing a lot of encrypted things online anyway (lots of websites are https-aware nowadays). As a result of plain L2TP being used, you can get away with hosting this on very weak hardware, and still get full speed. One day, I might write guides for how to use L2TP with, say, IPSEC enabled (using something other than A&A for the upstream L2TP service). You will not be able to use DNS until the L2TP is up, so we will use A&A’s IP address for l2tp.aa.net.uk directly, which is 90.155.53.19. Place the following contents: [lac aaisp] lns = 90.155.53.19 require authentication = no pppoptfile = /etc/ppp/options.aaisp Create this file, and place the following contents: NOTE: the name and password entries are your A&A login details for L2TP. +ipv6 ipv6cp-use-ipaddr name xyz@a.X password Your_xyz@A.X_password noauth ifname ppp-aaisp-l2tp PPP and L2TP are managed by pppd, which executes if up/down scripts when interfaces go up or down. We shall manipulate this accordingly: This file sets a default route on IPv6, but it can be (ab)used in general to handle L2TP/PPP going up/down. This file is for when the link goes up. A default route must be set! The file should contain this logic: #!/bin/bash /bin/logger $1 is up if [ $1 = "ppp-aaisp-l2tp" ]; then /bin/logger "AAISP over L2TP circuit is online; adding routes" /sbin/ip route add default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link /sbin/ip -6 route add default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link fi Don’t forget to make it executable: chmod 755 /etc/ppp/ipv6-up.d/0000-defaultroute The routes must be deleted, when the line goes down: #!/bin/bash /bin/logger $1 is down if [ $1 = "ppp-aaisp-l2tp" ]; then /bin/logger "AAISP over L2TP circuit is offline; removing routes" /sbin/ip route del default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link /sbin/ip -6 route del default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link fi Don’t forget to make this executable aswell: chmod 755 /etc/ppp/ipv6-down.d/0000-defaultroute You may notice that we have, thus far, not specified any way in which the L2TP tunnel connection is actually started. This will now be explained. Create the xl2tpd control file: mkdir -p /var/run/xl2tpd touch /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control Start the xl2tpd service: systemctl start xl2tpd Enable it at every boot: systemctl enable xl2tpd We now have the L2TP daemon starting automatically at boot time, but it will not automatically bring up your connection. The daemon monitors writes to a control file, which we just created at /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control. Tell the daemon to connect to aaisp: echo “c aaisp” > /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control To stop the L2TP connection, do this: echo “d aaisp” > /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control By running ip a, you will see the tunnel connection listed as ppp-aaisp-l2tp, but only when the PPP (over L2TP) connection is active. As you saw earlier, we went through the ifup/down scripts in Debian, that add/remove routes. You need to decide whether you want L2TP automatically starting in your router. In some situations, it may not actually be desirable for it to autostart, like if you just want to quickly test a new network but aren’t ready for it to go in production yet. You can find useful logs in /var/log/messages, for xl2tpd. Due to the way xl2tpd works (control files), I concluded that the best way to handle this is with crontab. As root, do: crontab -e In there, insert: * * * * * echo "c aaisp" > /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control You might also add something like this, for resolving domain names: * * * * * echo "nameserver 217.169.20.20" > /etc/resolv.conf This L2TP routing setup is a bit hacky, and this guide could use some refinement. The rule for resolvconf, as above, simply keeps DNS working. The nameserver IP used, in the above example, is provided by A&A for customers. Running the command when L2TP is up does nothing, and xl2tpd will simply exit on that run, while the tunnel remains open. When the tunnel is down, running that command will bring it back up. If your connection frequently has drop-outs of a few seconds, xl2tpd re-running every minute will give you a lot more unnecessary down time. It may be advisable to run every 5 seconds instead. The crontab file does not provide for this, allowing only per minute instructions in our case. You might simply run a script at boot time, that does it in a five-second loop. For example: #!/bin/sh while true do echo "c aaisp" > /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control sleep 5 done A more intelligent way might be to put, in the ifdown script as above, an instruction to run the above loop, but make the loop exit when the tunnel is up. That same modified script would also run at boot time. In this way, you might save an extra second or two, but I wouldn’t bother. You can simply hook up an ethernet switch, to the 2nd interface on your router, the one that has allocated IPv4/6 subnet addresses on it as per /etc/network/interfaces. Your host will then connect to that switch. On that ethernet switch, you will then set your host(s) to use an IP address from the /28 or /29 IPv4 subnet. You may even have a bigger subnet than that, if you asked A&A nicely. You can also use IPv6, but without SLAAC; simply set as many static IPv6 addresses that you want, on the host. With this routing setup, dual stack IPv4 and IPv6 is possible, for any host connected to it. The internet should Just Work on the router itself. No DHCP or NAT is running, in this configuration; perhaps a guide could be written for that, but for this exact setup as described on the page, you can simply specify the following as static IP address: IP (host): any unused IP address (v4 or v6) on the subnet A&A gave you. Example (for libreboot.org): 81.187.172.132 and 2001:8b0:b95:1bb5::4 gateway: the IP of the L2TP router, on LAN side. In the example above, this would be 81.187.172.129 and 2001:8b0:b95:1bb5::1 netmask (IPv4): 255.255.255.240 on my /28 subnet. If you have a /29, it should be 255.255.255.248 broadcast (IPv4): in my case, I’m on 81.187.172.128/28, so the broadcast address would be 81.187.191.143; 128 is 10000000 in binary, and 32-28 is 4, so we mask the 4 least significant bits which becomes 10001111, which is 143. You need to do the maths, for your specific IP and subnet size. prefix (IPv6): 64 Again, there is no DHCP on this network; additionally, we are not running a DNS resolver (you could run one, if you wish). You must specify one manually. Many resolvers exist. A&A provide them, for customers: 217.169.20.20 217.269.20.21 2001:8b0::2020 2001:8b0::2021 You should configure SSH to accept keys only and (optional) only listen on a local IP address (e.g. 10 network). This is beyond the scope of the article, but it’s quite trivial to set up. e.g. ListenAddress 10.0.0.42 The following commands may be useful later, to debug issues: ip route ip -6 route ping 8.8.8.8 ping6 2001:4860:4860::8888 tcpdump -ni eno0 Your main ISP (that you use to then run L2TP through) most likely doesn’t support higher than 1500 MTU, if that. Your L2TP connection will add bytes in a frame, so the encapsulated PPP connection will have a lower MTU. There is no way to avoid this, unless you have a hypothetical ISP that can give you, say, 1540 MTU or something like that. Anyway, the result is that your packets will be fragmented. In your A&A control panel login (see: https://control.aa.net.uk/), you can set MTU manually but I just recommend leaving it on auto. If you see an MTU of, say, 1460, on your PPP connection (when SSH’d into the router and running ip a or something), don’t worry, it’s normal. Just let your router handle it, it’s what Linux was born to do. Sometimes called reverse DNS. In an IP address, the PTR record resolves back to an arbitrary domain name which can be set. Typically, your ISP will assign one and that’s all you get, but A&A lets you change it in the control panel: https://control.aa.net.uk/ You must get your domain name added to your login, even if it’s not actually registered with A&A. Simply email their tech team and ask them to do it. You could also just ask them to set the PTR records. For example, A/AAAA records in your DNS for foo.bar.com might point to one of your IPs, and then you’d make that IP point back to foo.bar.com. You can do this for an IPv4 and an IPv6 address that A&A assigns to you. This can be very useful when running mail servers, precisely because you can make the same entry for both IPv4 and IPv6. For example, my mail server has the PTR record, on IPv4 and IPv6, of libreland.libreboot.org and I specify this in my mail server plus DNS server configurations; the IP is also set in my SPF record, with A/AAAA records for that IP pointing to libreland.libreboot.org, so that everything matches up. This, plus other things like setting proper DKIM record, is essential when running a mail server, because a lot of services (like GMail) will block you on suspicion of spam if these are misconfigured. My next guide may in fact be how to set up a mail server! Also DNS and web, etc. I will not configure a firewall on this network. I always get an IPv4 subnet from a&a either on hardlines or L2TP, and I run an open network. The router is always hardened to only allow local SSH connections, or SSH turned off, for security. No NAT/DHCP either. If local hosts want to firewall themselves, they can, and they can provide that stuff. I really don’t see the point in using DHCP for public IPv4 subnets. If I want NAT/DHCP inside such a network, I usually plug in an OpenWRT router and set a static IP on the WAN port for that. I also use OpenWRT routers to in this way, when I want to set up a WiFi connection behind A&A. Essentially, I like my main network to be “invisible”. Just plug in and set an IP (from the public subnet) and you’re good to go. This assumes you have good physical security and/or you trust the people that have access to it. In short, this is a real internet connection. Anything you plug into this network will be directly on the internet. You should consider your security model, when doing this. It is especially important to consider physical security; who do you trust, if you’re running this at your company (or even your own home)? You should not connect anything insecure directly to this main network. For iexample, your playstation or proprietary shitware Windows PC are not to be trusted. A secure linux/BSD machine, assuming you’re competent, is absolutely fine. This setup is intended for sysadmins who really want to host lots of servers on their home network. You might configure codel which is nice for QoS but that’s beyond the scope of this article. The /tmp, /var/run and /var/lock directories should also be tmpfs. This isn’t strictly necessary, but for a high-performance machine it might be desirable, especially for something like this. If you’re running this on really slow hardware, you might consider that, but you must also take memory usage into account when relying on tmpfs. Most people assume that a router is a piece of hardware, but that’s not true. The router is actually software, and the hardware is just what that software runs on. Almost anything can be a router, just like anything can be on a cob in that one episode of Rick and Morty. The laptop in the photo is my router, configured in exactly the way this guide describes.

blocks.html_en: Have you ever wanted to host a server at home or in your office, but you can’t because the ISP won’t give you static IPs? Are you behind a CGNAT? This guide is for you. It will teach you how to route static IPv4 and (native) IPv6 addresses to your network, with hosts directly pingable on the internet and all ports open. With this guide, you won’t need to host your software project on github anymore, because you can instead install gitea/cgit with a mailing list on your raspberry pi and host it in your basement or living room!

blocks.html_en: I recently moved libreboot.org hosting to a much faster network than what it had before, but the new ISP doesn’t assign static IPv4 or IPv6 subnets on the line, and it has all kinds of restrictions, though speed, uptime and latency are all excellent. I decided therefore to set up a tunnel connection using Andrews & Arnold Ltd (A&A) L2TP tunnel service. This is basically similar to most VPN services, but you get a lot more freedom and flexibility e.g. IPv4 subnets (for example, you could host your own DNS on this).

blocks.html_en: L2TP is a protocol used for to tunnel traffic on the internet. It’s quite commonly used by ISPs to connect customers up to their backend, where they then provide a PPP login.

blocks.html_en: So long as you have an ethernet port available to use for internet, your tunnel router can work nicely. 大多数人认为路由器是一个硬件，但事实并非如此。 路由器实际上是软件，而硬件正是软件运行的基础。 几乎任何东西都可以成为路由器，就像瑞克和莫蒂那一集中的任何东西都可以是玉米棒子一样。 照片中的笔记本电脑是我的路由器，完全按照本指南描述的方式进行配置。

您是否曾经想在家里或办公室托管服务器，但由于 ISP 不会为您提供静态 IP 而无法实现？ 您支持 CGNAT 吗？ 本指南适合您。 它将教您如何将静态 IPv4 和（本机）IPv6 地址路由到您的网络，其中主机可以直接在互联网上执行 ping 操作并且所有端口都打开。 有了本指南，您将不再需要在 github 上托管您的软件项目，因为您可以在树莓派上安装带有邮件列表的 gitea/cgit 并将其托管在您的地下室或客厅！

我最近将 libreboot.org 托管到比以前更快的网络，但新的 ISP 不会在线分配静态 IPv4 或 IPv6 子网，并且它有各种限制，尽管速度、正常运行时间和延迟都非常好。 因此，我决定使用 Andrews & Arnold Ltd (A&A) L2TP 隧道服务建立隧道连接。 这基本上与大多数 VPN 服务相似，但您可以获得更多的自由度和灵活性，例如IPv4 子网（例如，您可以在此托管您自己的 DNS）。

它也可以仅用于正常的日常互联网任务。 A&A 为您提供未经过滤、不受任何形式限制的服务。

根据您的发行版调整本指南。 基本上我们想要做的就是通过 L2TP 进行 PPP 并在 Linux 中启用数据包转发，以便数据包可以在两个接口之间传递。 然后我们设定路线。 我们将有这些接口：

  • WAN 端口（以太网）- 上游 ISP
  • 隧道端口（ppp over l2tp） - 物理上通过 WAN 端口
  • LAN 端口（以太网）- 数据包仅在其与隧道之间路由，而不是直接在 WAN 端口之间路由。 路线相应设置。

L2TP 是一种用于在互联网上传输流量的协议。 ISP 经常使用它来将客户连接到后端，然后在后端提供 PPP 登录。

只要您有一个可用于互联网的以太网端口，您的隧道路由器就可以正常工作。 如果需要，您可以在另一台计算机上设置 WiFi 连接或 4G 网络，通过 RJ45 以太网端口共享该连接以供 L2TP 路由器连接；例如，树莓派 USB 通过加密狗连接到 4G LTE 服务，可能通过以太网在 NAT+DHCP 上分配 IP。

流量将通过静态路由强制发送至 A&A 的 L2TP 隧道服务器。 这样，所有流量都将通过 L2TP，而不是其他流量。 它与您的主网络完全隔离。 通过此设置，您可以将服务器托管在任何地方，并且可以非常轻松地移动它们。

您需要一台带有 2 个以太网接口 (RJ45) 的计算机。 然后您需要在其上运行 Linux 或 BSD。 出于本教程的目的，我将告诉您如何配置 Debian Linux，但此处的信息可以适用于任何其他系统。 我真的只建议在 BSD 或 Linux 上托管它。

就我而言，我有这些物理接口：

  • enp14s0 通过 NAT 地址配置到普通 ISP 路由器，并通过静态路由配置到 A&A 的 L2TP 服务器。 客户端L2TP应通过此连接
  • eno0 用于将 IP 从 L2TP 路由到交换机。 这基本上就是我的 LAN 端口

您的可能会有所不同，因此请相应地进行调整。

当您第一次在路由器上安装 Debian 时，您也可以只使用网络安装程序。 仅安装基本系统（在taskel中选择的标准系统实用程序）。 如果您愿意，也可以启用 SSH。

在实际配置路由之前，您的 Debian 计算机必须具有互联网，以便您可以下载软件包。 或者，您可能已将 apt 配置为从安装介质中获取它们。 这取决于你，真的。

您必须安装这些软件包：

apt-get install ppp pppoe xl2tpd iproute2 tcpdump net-tools resolvconf

您应该在执行其他操作之前安装这些软件包。 只需通过 DHCP 或其他方式连接并安装它们即可。 您还可以从 Debian 安装介质中获取它们。

如果你需要一个像样的文本编辑器，我可以推荐 Vim。 尽管看起来很可耻，但 Debian 默认情况下并不安装它！

在继续之前，请确保您已安装上面列出的软件包。 此时，我们直接开始并配置一切。

出于我们的目的，路由器的 WAN 端将通过 NAT、通过主 ISP 网络连接到互联网，但我们不会使用 DHCP。 相反，将指定静态 (NAT) IP 地址，但没有网关；这样做时，不会设置默认路由，但我们将设置静态路由。

静态路由只会通过网关 IP 将流量路由到 90.155.53.19，即 A&A 的 L2TP 服务器，在我的情况下为 10.42.0.1，但在您的情况下可能是 192.168.1.1。 你必须相应地适应。

通过这样设置静态路由，我们只能在隧道连接断开时才能连接到 A&A L2TP。 当它启动时，我们仍然没有默认路由，但随后我们添加了一条默认路由，通过 L2TP 通过 PPP 隧道。 这样，所有流量（除了直接到 90.155.53.19 的流量）都将通过 L2TP 隧道，而不是您的主要上游 ISP（例如 Virgin、Sky、TalkTalk）。 通过这样做，我们确保所有流量仅正确通过 A&A。

我们直接使用 A&A 的 IP 地址的原因是因为当 L2TP 隧道关闭时我们没有 DNS。

请阅读下面示例中的注释。 它们很重要。 您必须根据您的目的调整以下配置：

source /etc/network/interfaces.d/*

# The loopback network interface
auto lo
iface lo inet loopback

# NOTE: 10.42.0.116 is the normal gateway router, LAN side,
# not anything l2tp-related.
# the 10 addresses below would likely be `192.168.x.x/24` in your case
# adapt accordingly

# NOTE: the IPs on eno0 are /28 subnet ones, assigned by a&a for my l2tp service
# you must adapt these for your own line. please note also a&a typically
# offers a /29 for l2tp but they gave me a /28; for a /29, you should
# use netmask 255.255.255.248, but in my case i specified 255.255.255.240

auto enp14s0
allow-hotplug enp14s0
iface enp14s0 inet static
       address 10.42.0.116
       netmask 255.255.255.0
       network 10.42.0.0
       # gateway 10.42.0.1 # we will set a custom route instead. see below
       broadcast 10.42.0.255
       up /sbin/ip route add 90.155.53.19/32 via 10.42.0.1 dev enp14s0

# LAN
auto eno0
iface eno0 inet static 
   address 81.187.172.129
   netmask 255.255.255.240 
   dns-nameservers 217.169.20.20 217.169.20.21

iface eno0 inet6 static 
   address  2001:8b0:b95:1bb5::1
   netmask 64 
   dns-nameservers 2001:8b0::2020 2001:8b0::2021

# NOTE: because above, we are forcing everything to go over L2TP, we will
# not have DNS until the L2TP is up. this is why the IP address of A&A's
# L2TP router is used directly!

# NOTE: no hardline so PPP not configured here. This is handled via xl2tpd

注意：IP 地址 90.155.53.19 是 l2tp.aa.net.uk 解析的地址，由于在设置 L2TP 时该网络初始化期间缺少名称解析，因此应直接将其用于我们的目的。 我们在 enp14s0 上设置的静态路由确保我们在 WAN 端有互联网（到主 ISP，而不是 A&A），假设（物理）主网络本身正常工作。

您必须允许数据包转发，以便流量可以在两个网络接口之间流动。 编辑这个文件：

取消注释这一行：

#net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

这行（注意：禁用无状态地址自动配置）

#net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1

这些行应该如下所示：

net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1

现在运行：

系统控制-p

最后一个命令现在只是应用它，但这也将在系统的每次引导期间应用。

我们像强硬路线一样配置 PPP，这似乎有悖常理，但这对于下一步很重要。 A&A 提供无需身份验证的 L2TP，但随后您可以通过通过 L2TP 路由的 PPP 进行身份验证。 当您使用 A&A 时，您的（公共）IP 地址是通过 PPP 分配的。 他们的硬线服务器（例如 VDSL/FTTP）也是如此。

Debian 内核应该已经具有正确的模块，但否则您必须确保在内核配置中启用 CONFIG_PPPOL2TP 和 CONFIG_L2TP 选项。

应该注意的是，A&A L2TP 服务（截至目前）目前没有 IPSEC 或其他加密（例如wireguard）。 这不太理想，但无论如何您可能会在网上做很多加密的事情（现在很多网站都支持 https）。

由于使用了普通的 L2TP，您可以在非常弱的硬件上托管它，并且仍然获得全速。 有一天，我可能会编写有关如何在启用 IPSEC 的情况下使用 L2TP 的指南（对上游 L2TP 服务使用 A&A 之外的其他内容）。

在 L2TP 启动之前，您将无法使用 DNS，因此我们将直接使用 A&A 的 IP 地址作为 l2tp.aa.net.uk，即 90.155.53.19。

放置以下内容：

[lac aaisp]
lns = 90.155.53.19
require authentication = no
pppoptfile = /etc/ppp/options.aaisp

创建此文件，并放置以下内容：

注意：名称和密码条目是您的 L2TP 的 A&A 登录详细信息。

+ipv6
ipv6cp-use-ipaddr
name xyz@a.X
password Your_xyz@A.X_password
noauth
ifname ppp-aaisp-l2tp

PPP 和 L2TP 由 pppd 管理，当接口打开或关闭时，它会执行 if up/down 脚本。 我们将相应地操纵它：

该文件在 IPv6 上设置默认路由，但通常可以（滥用）使用它来处理 L2TP/PPP 上行/下行。 该文件用于链接建立时的文件。 必须设置默认路由！

该文件应包含以下逻辑：

#!/bin/bash
/bin/logger $1 is up
if [ $1 = "ppp-aaisp-l2tp" ]; then
	/bin/logger "AAISP over L2TP circuit is online; adding routes"
	/sbin/ip route add default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link
	/sbin/ip -6 route add default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link
fi

不要忘记使其可执行：

chmod 755 /etc/ppp/ipv6-up.d/0000-defaultroute

当线路中断时，必须删除路由：

#!/bin/bash
/bin/logger $1 is down
if [ $1 = "ppp-aaisp-l2tp" ]; then
	/bin/logger "AAISP over L2TP circuit is offline; removing routes"
	/sbin/ip route del default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link
	/sbin/ip -6 route del default dev ppp-aaisp-l2tp scope link
fi

不要忘记也使此可执行文件：

chmod 755 /etc/ppp/ipv6-down.d/0000-defaultroute

您可能会注意到，到目前为止，我们还没有指定 L2TP 隧道连接实际启动的任何方式。 现在对此进行解释。

创建 xl2tpd 控制文件：

mkdir -p /var/run/xl2tpd touch /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control

启动 xl2tpd 服务：

systemctl 启动 xl2tpd

每次启动时启用它：

systemctl 启用 xl2tpd

现在，L2TP 守护进程在启动时自动启动，但它不会自动建立连接。 守护进程监视对控制文件的写入，该文件是我们刚刚在 /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control 创建的。

告诉守护进程连接到 aaisp：

回声“c aaisp”> /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control

要停止 L2TP 连接，请执行以下操作：

回声“d aaisp”> /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control

通过运行 ip a，您将看到列为 ppp-aaisp-l2tp 的隧道连接，但前提是 PPP（通过 L2TP）连接处于活动状态。 正如您之前看到的，我们浏览了 Debian 中的 ifup/down 脚本，用于添加/删除路由。

您需要决定是否希望 L2TP 在路由器中自动启动。 在某些情况下，实际上可能并不需要它自动启动，例如，如果您只想快速测试新网络但尚未准备好将其投入生产。

您可以在 /var/log/messages 中找到 xl2tpd 的有用日志。

由于 xl2tpd 的工作方式（控制文件），我得出结论，处理此问题的最佳方法是使用 crontab。 作为 root，执行以下操作：

crontab -e

在其中插入：

* * * * * echo "c aaisp" > /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control

您还可以添加类似的内容来解析域名：

* * * * * echo "nameserver 217.169.20.20" > /etc/resolv.conf

这个 L2TP 路由设置有点老套，本指南可以进行一些改进。 如上所述，resolvconf 的规则只是保持 DNS 正常工作。 上例中使用的名称服务器 IP 由 A&A 为客户提供。

当 L2TP 启动时运行该命令不会执行任何操作，xl2tpd 将在该运行中退出，而隧道保持打开状态。 当隧道关闭时，运行该命令会将其恢复。

如果您的连接经常出现几秒钟的中断，xl2tpd 每分钟重新运行会给您带来更多不必要的停机时间。

建议每 5 秒运行一次。 crontab 文件没有提供这一点，在我们的例子中只允许每分钟指令。

您可以简单地在启动时运行一个脚本，它会在五秒的循环中完成。 例如：

#!/bin/sh

while true
do
	echo "c aaisp" > /var/run/xl2tpd/l2tp-control
	sleep 5
done

更明智的方法可能是在上面的 ifdown 脚本中放置一条运行上述循环的指令，但在隧道启动时退出循环。 相同的修改后的脚本也将在启动时运行。 这样，你可能会多节省一两秒钟，但我不会打扰。

您只需将以太网交换机连接到路由器上的第二个接口，该接口已根据 /etc/network/interfaces 为其分配了 IPv4/6 子网地址。 然后您的主机将连接到该交换机。

然后，在该以太网交换机上，您将主机设置为使用 /28 或 /29 IPv4 子网中的 IP 地址。 如果您很好地询问 A&A，您甚至可能拥有比这更大的子网。 您也可以使用 IPv6，但没有 SLAAC；只需在主机上设置所需数量的静态 IPv6 地址即可。

通过此路由设置，对于连接到它的任何主机，双堆栈 IPv4 和 IPv6 都是可能的。

互联网应该只在路由器本身上工作。 在此配置中，没有运行 DHCP 或 NAT；也许可以为此编写指南，但对于页面上描述的确切设置，您可以简单地将以下内容指定为静态 IP 地址：

  • IP（主机）：A&A 为您提供的子网上任何未使用的 IP 地址（v4 或 v6）。 示例（对于 libreboot.org）：81.187.172.132 和 2001:8b0:b95:1bb5::4
  • gateway：LAN侧L2TP路由器的IP。 在上面的示例中，这将是 81.187.172.129 和 2001:8b0:b95:1bb5::1
  • 网络掩码 (IPv4)：我的 /28 子网上的 255.255.255.240。 如果您有 /29，则应为 255.255.255.248
  • 广播 (IPv4)：在我的例子中，我使用的是 81.187.172.128/28，因此广播地址为 81.187.191.143； 128在二进制中是10000000，32-28是4，所以我们屏蔽掉4个最低有效位，变成10001111，也就是143。 您需要针对您的特定 IP 和子网大小进行数学计算。
  • 前缀 (IPv6)：64

同样，该网络上没有 DHCP；此外，我们没有运行 DNS 解析器（如果您愿意，您可以运行一个）。 您必须手动指定一个。 存在许多解析器。 A&A 为客户提供：

  • 217.169.20.20
  • 217.269.20.21
  • 2001:8b0::2020
  • 2001:8b0::2021

您应该将 SSH 配置为仅接受密钥并且（可选）仅侦听本地 IP 地址（例如 10 网络）。 这超出了本文的范围，但设置起来非常简单。

e.g.

监听地址 10.0.0.42

以下命令可能会在稍后用于调试问题时有用：

ip route
ip -6 route
ping 8.8.8.8
ping6 2001:4860:4860::8888
tcpdump -ni eno0

如果是的话，您的主要 ISP（您用来运行 L2TP 的）很可能不支持高于 1500 MTU。 您的 L2TP 连接将在帧中添加字节，因此封装的 PPP 连接将具有较低的 MTU。 没有办法避免这种情况，除非您有一个假设的 ISP 可以为您提供 1540 MTU 或类似的值。

无论如何，结果是你的数据包将被碎片化。 在您的 A&A 控制面板登录中（请参阅：https://control.aa.net.uk/），您可以手动设置 MTU，但我建议将其保留为自动。

如果您在 PPP 连接上看到 MTU 为 1460（当通过 SSH 连接到路由器并运行 ip a 或其他命令时），请不要担心，这是正常的。 让你的路由器来处理它，这就是 Linux 的诞生。

有时称为反向 DNS。

在 IP 地址中，PTR 记录解析回可以设置的任意域名。 通常，您的 ISP 会分配一个，这就是您所获得的全部，但 A&A 允许您在控制面板中更改它：https://control.aa.net.uk/

您必须将您的域名添加到您的登录信息中，即使它实际上并未在 A&A 注册。 只需向他们的技术团队发送电子邮件并要求他们这样做即可。 您也可以要求他们设置 PTR 记录。

例如，您的 DNS 中 foo.bar.com 的 A/AAAA 记录可能指向您的某个 IP，然后您可以将该 IP 指向回 foo.bar.com。 您可以对 A&A 分配给您的 IPv4 和 IPv6 地址执行此操作。

这在运行邮件服务器时非常有用，因为您可以为 IPv4 和 IPv6 创建相同的条目。 例如，我的邮件服务器在 IPv4 和 IPv6 上具有 libreland.libreboot.org 的 PTR 记录，并且我在邮件服务器和 DNS 服务器配置中指定了该记录； IP 也在我的 SPF 记录中设置，该 IP 的 A/AAAA 记录指向 libreland.libreboot.org，以便一切都匹配。 这一点，再加上设置正确的 DKIM 记录等其他内容，在运行邮件服务器时至关重要，因为如果配置错误，许多服务（例如 GMail）会因怀疑垃圾邮件而阻止您。

我的下一个指南实际上可能是如何设置邮件服务器！ 还有 DNS 和 Web 等。

我不会在此网络上配置防火墙。 我总是通过硬线或 L2TP 从 a&a 获得 IPv4 子网，并且运行开放网络。 为了安全起见，路由器始终经过强化，只允许本地 SSH 连接，或者关闭 SSH。

也没有 NAT/DHCP。 如果本地主机想要自己设置防火墙，他们可以，而且他们可以提供这些东西。 我真的不明白对公共 IPv4 子网使用 DHCP 有何意义。

如果我想在这样的网络中使用 NAT/DHCP，我通常会插入 OpenWRT 路由器并在 WAN 端口上设置静态 IP。 当我想在 A&A 后面设置 WiFi 连接时，我也以这种方式使用 OpenWRT 路由器。

本质上，我喜欢我的主网络是“隐形的”。 只需插入并设置一个 IP（来自公共子网）即可开始使用。 这假设您拥有良好的物理安全性和/或您信任有权访问它的人。

简而言之，这是真正的互联网连接。 您插入该网络的任何内容都将直接连接到互联网。 执行此操作时，您应该考虑您的安全模型。 考虑物理安全尤为重要；如果您在公司（甚至您自己的家）运行此程序，您信任谁？

您不应该将任何不安全的东西直接连接到该主网络。 例如，您的游戏机或专有的垃圾 Windows PC 不值得信任。 假设您有能力，一台安全的 linux/BSD 机器绝对没问题。 此设置适用于真正希望在其家庭网络上托管大量服务器的系统管理员。

您可以配置有利于 QoS 的 codel，但这超出了本文的范围。

/tmp、/var/run 和 /var/lock 目录也应该是 tmpfs。 这并不是绝对必要的，但对于高性能机器来说，这可能是可取的，尤其是对于这样的事情。

如果您在非常慢的硬件上运行它，您可能会考虑这一点，但在依赖 tmpfs 时还必须考虑内存使用情况。
